articles.author: Omar Zahouri
articles.description:
We don't have a shortage of AI coding tools.
We have a shortage of simple workflows.
Why should building software with AI require:
Accounts.
What if you could simply bring your own API key and start building?
That's the philosophy behind NullCry.
You choose the model.
You bring the key.
NullCry works with the project.
Multiple files.
I'm not trying to convince everyone that NullCry is the answer.
I'm trying to start a conversation about what AI development should actually look like.
If you were designing an AI coding tool from scratch, what would you remove?
— Omar Zahouri
https://nullcry.com
articles.title: Maybe developers don't need more AI. Maybe they need less friction.

articles.author: horlartundhey
articles.description:
The first assignment was the least glamorous and probably the most useful. Ansible can't run natively on Windows, so the controller lives in Ubuntu under WSL. I installed Ansible, ansible-lint, yamllint and pre-commit inside a Python virtual environment, pinned the versions in requirements.txt, and set up SSH keys, an agent, and Git hooks that lint every YAML file before a commit.
Four small problems each taught me something:
My project was on the Windows drive. From Linux, every file there looks world-writable, and Ansible deliberately ignores an ansible.cfg in a world-writable folder. It doesn't warn you loudly, it just runs with defaults. Moving the project into the Linux home folder fixed it.
A hidden character broke the pre-commit config. I had generated a version number with a comman…
articles.title: Ansible From a Blank Workstation to a Deployment I Reviewed Before It Ran

articles.author: Omar Zahouri
articles.description:
Most developers trust AI to write a function.
But would you trust it with your entire project?
Multiple files.
That's a very different problem.
And that's exactly where I think AI development is heading.
NullCry is my attempt at building for that direction.
Instead of treating every prompt as an isolated coding task, NullCry is designed to work with the project as a whole.
Bring your own API key.
I'm not claiming AI can replace developers.
I'm asking whether AI should be treated as a code generator at all.
Maybe the better model is an AI that works alongside the entire project.
Would you trust an AI with your codebase?
Yes or no — and why?
— Omar Zahouri
https://nullcry.com
articles.title: Would you trust AI with your entire codebase?

articles.author: KillianBerg5391
articles.description:
Short answer: Downtime monitoring for SaaS applications with multiple microservices works best as layered evidence: service heartbeats, a synthetic checkout journey, and probes from multiple regions, interpreted together before anyone declares the application down.
The least complex design that gives a trustworthy answer is layered. A checkout monitor should answer one operational question: can a customer complete the purchase right now? Treat each result as a signal, then interpret the signals together before declaring the checkout down.
That last step matters. A payment service can be healthy while an API gateway, inventory dependency, or browser-facing path is failing. A single green endpoint is not proof that checkout works; a single red dependency is not automatically a customer-visib…
articles.title: Downtime Monitoring for SaaS Applications with Multiple Microservices — Signal Design

articles.author: Omar Zahouri
articles.description:
I didn't start NullCry with a team.
I didn't have investors.
I didn't have a big marketing budget.
I had an idea, a browser, and a lot of time.
I wanted to build something I would actually use as a developer:
An AI tool that works with the project itself, not just isolated pieces of code.
So I built NullCry.
Today it can work across multiple files, continue existing projects, make cross-file changes, fix problems, and generate complete projects.
The interesting part?
I'm still building it independently.
No big company behind it.
Just one developer trying to see how far the idea can go.
Maybe it will succeed.
But I think independent developers should build ambitious things anyway.
So I'm putting NullCry in front of the developer community.
If you were building this from zero, what would you change first?
— Omar Zahouri
https://nullcry.com
articles.title: I built an AI developer tool with almost no money.

articles.description:
I built a booking app for gyms with React, TanStack Start and Supabase. The part that looked easy and wasn't: two people booking the same slot at the same moment.
This post explains the approach I ended up with, with a simplified version of the code.
The problem
A client opens the booking page, picks a service, a date and a time slot. Two clients can do this for the same trainer and the same slot within milliseconds of each other.
If your app does this in two steps:
SELECT to check the slot is free
then both requests can pass step 1 before either one reaches step 2. Result: a double booking.
Checking in the frontend or in your API code doesn't fix it, because the race happens between your two queries.
Why not just a unique constraint?
A unique constraint works if every booking uses exactly…
articles.title: How I prevent double bookings in Postgres (advisory locks + Supabase)

AI can write impressive code.
But give it a real project with 30 files, dependencies, existing logic, and changes happening across the codebase...
Suddenly, "write me some code" isn't enough.

What depends on what?
That's the problem I'm trying to solve with NullCry.

A project-level AI development workflow.
Bring your own API key.
I'm building NullCry independently.
And honestly, I want developers to challenge this idea.
Is project-level AI actually the future?
Or are we overcomplicating something that should stay simple?

articles.author: Etairos.ai
articles.description:
TL;DR




what: SonicWall disclosed CVE-2026-19868, an SSL-VPN authentication bypass in SonicOS that lets attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method skip SAML controls, and CISA has confirmed it is exploited in the wild.
impact: On SAML-configured SSL-VPN deployments, the SAML-enforced MFA layer can be sidestepped, turning a single stolen password into remote network access.
fix: Upgrade to SonicOS 7.3.4-7013 (Gen7) or 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8), which fix CVE-2026-19868 and six other flaws; SonicWall says no workarounds exist.
who: Organizations running SonicOS Gen7 7.3.3-7015 and earlier or Gen8 8.2.2-8015 and earlier with SSL-VPN configured for SAML authentication.
Attackers are using a SonicWall SSL-VPN flaw to get past the control many organizations count on to sto…
articles.title: SonicWall CVE-2026-19868: SSL-VPN SAML MFA Bypass Exploited in the Wild

articles.author: Omar Zahouri
articles.description:
I don't think developers need another AI chatbot.
We already have enough of them.
What developers need is AI that can actually work with the software they're building.
Not just:
"Write me a function."
But:
"Here is my project. Understand it. Change these files. Fix what breaks. Continue from where we stopped. Keep the whole thing working."
That's the idea behind NullCry.
NullCry is an AI project development tool designed to work across real projects and multiple files.
You bring your own API key.
No login.
I'm building it independently, and I'm deliberately challenging the way AI development tools are being packaged today.
Maybe the idea is wrong.
Maybe developers don't want this.
If you disagree, tell me exactly why.
I'd rather get a brutal technical opinion than another "looks cool."
— Omar Zahouri
https://nullcry.com
articles.title: I don't think developers need another AI chatbot.
